scenarios.title: Why a sigma-algebra?
scenarios.situation: A junior analyst says probability is simple: assign every event a number between 0 and 1 that sums to 1. Your team models continuous asset prices, so the sample space is the real line — uncountably many outcomes, with events like 'the price lands in [100, 105)' that must combine under unions and complements.
scenarios.prompt: Why can't we just define probability on EVERY subset of the real line?
choices: A sigma-algebra (closed under complements and countable unions) is required for the probability axioms to hold consistently; on an uncountable space, no assignment of probabilities to every subset satisfies countable additivity — some subsets are provably non-measurable.
Because computing probabilities on every subset is too slow for real-time trading systems.
Because the real line has too many points, so we only need the Borel sets to keep the data files small.
Because regulators require a named sigma-algebra on all model documentation.
scenarios.why: Probability's axioms (nonnegativity, normalization, countable additivity) only make sense on a collection of sets closed under the operations the axioms use: complements and countable unions. On the continuum, assigning a consistent probability to literally every subset is impossible — there exist non-measurable sets — so measure theory restricts probability to a sigma-algebra, typically the Borel sets, where the axioms hold.
scenarios.hint: Which axiom of probability needs you to take a countable union of events?

scenarios.title: Expectation as integral
scenarios.situation: A desk quant prices a simple contract that pays $10 if a coin lands heads and $0 if tails, repeated many times. A new hire computes the 'average payout' as (10 + 0) / 2 = $5 and asks why the probability course keeps insisting expectation is 'integration with respect to a probability measure.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the measure-theoretic view of expectation, in plain terms?
choices: Expectation is the integral of the random variable (a measurable function from the sample space to the reals) with respect to the probability measure: E[X] = integral X dP — the weighted average over outcomes, which reduces to a sum for discrete variables and a density-weighted integral for continuous ones.
Expectation is the median of the distribution, computed by integrating the CDF from 0 to 1.
Expectation only applies to discrete variables; continuous ones use the mode instead.
Expectation is defined by Monte Carlo simulation, so no closed form is ever needed.
scenarios.why: Viewing X as a measurable function and E[X] as its integral against P unifies the discrete sum and the continuous density integral into one definition — and it is the definition that lets you prove the theorems quants rely on, like linearity of expectation and dominated convergence, without re-proving them for each distribution family.
scenarios.hint: What does X as a function map FROM and TO?

scenarios.title: The absorbing Markov chain
scenarios.situation: A credit-risk model tracks a bond's rating each quarter as a Markov chain over states {A, B, Default}, where Default is absorbing (once defaulted, the bond stays defaulted). The risk team needs the probability that a currently A-rated bond eventually defaults — not the probability after exactly N quarters, but ever.
scenarios.prompt: How do you compute the eventual-default probability from state A?
choices: Solve the first-step equations: let h_A, h_B be the eventual-default probabilities; then h_A = p_AA*h_A + p_AB*h_B + p_ADefault*1 and h_B = p_BA*h_A + p_BB*h_B + p_BDefault*1, and solve the linear system for h_A (with h_Default = 1).
Raise the transition matrix to the 4th power and read off the entry for (A, Default).
Compute the stationary distribution of the chain and take the Default component.
Simulate one path of the chain for 100 steps and use its endpoint.
scenarios.why: First-step analysis conditions on the first transition and writes the absorption probability as a weighted average of the same quantity from the successor states, yielding a linear system. This is exact for eventual absorption, unlike a fixed-horizon power (which truncates the tail) or the stationary distribution (which here is degenerate at the absorbing state and carries no information about where the chain started).
scenarios.hint: Write the equation for h_A by conditioning on the first step.

scenarios.title: Discounting the cash flow
scenarios.situation: A hiring committee interviews you for a quant-adjacent role and hands you a warm-up: a project pays $110 in one year and $121 in two years. The risk-free rate is 10% per year, compounded annually. They ask what the project is worth today and whether you'd pay $195 for it.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct present value, and the decision?
choices: PV = 110/1.1 + 121/1.1^2 = 100 + 100 = $200, so paying $195 is a $5 positive-NPV deal — take it.
PV = 110 + 121 = $231 discounted by 10% once = $210; take it.
scenarios.why: Each cash flow is discounted by the number of periods until it arrives: 110/1.1 = 100 and 121/1.21 = 100, so PV = $200. NPV = 200 − 195 = +$5 > 0, so the investment creates value. The common traps are discounting the two-year flow by only one year, or discounting the total by a single factor.
scenarios.hint: How many years until the $121 arrives?

scenarios.title: Why Brownian motion?
scenarios.situation: A researcher proposes modeling a stock price as a random walk with fixed-size steps each minute. A senior quant rejects it and says the desk standard is geometric Brownian motion: dS = mu*S*dt + sigma*S*dW. The researcher asks what specifically Brownian motion buys them that the fixed-step walk doesn't.
scenarios.prompt: What is the essential mathematical property of Brownian motion that makes it the standard driver?
choices: Brownian motion has continuous paths with independent, stationary, normally distributed increments — the continuous-time limit of the random walk — and the geometric form (scaling the noise by the price S) keeps prices positive and produces log-normal returns, matching the multiplicative nature of compounding.
Brownian motion guarantees the price never goes negative because the steps shrink over time.
Brownian motion is used because its increments are predictable one step ahead, which makes hedging exact.
Brownian motion was chosen historically and any symmetric process would price options identically.
scenarios.why: Brownian motion is the scaling limit of the simple random walk (Donsker's theorem): continuous paths, independent increments, W_t − W_s ~ N(0, t−s). Geometric Brownian motion multiplies that noise by the price level, so returns — not absolute moves — are normal, prices stay positive, and compounding is multiplicative. The fixed-step walk is the discrete skeleton; Brownian motion is its continuous-time limit, which is what makes stochastic calculus (Ito's lemma) applicable.
scenarios.hint: If you shrink the step size and speed up the steps, what does the random walk converge to?

scenarios.title: The one-step binomial
scenarios.situation: A stock trades at $100. In one period it moves to $110 (up) or $90 (down). The risk-free rate is 5% per period. You must price a European call with strike $100 expiring in one period. A colleague prices it as the 'expected payoff' using the real-world 50/50 probabilities: 0.5*10 + 0.5*0 = $5, discounted to $4.76.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct arbitrage-free price?
choices: About $7.14: the risk-neutral probability is p = (1.05x100 - 90)/(110 - 90) = 0.75, so the call value is (0.75x10 + 0.25x0)/1.05 = 7.5/1.05 = $7.14 — exactly the cost of the replicating portfolio (delta = 0.5 shares), which is why no other price is arbitrage-free.
The colleague is right: $4.76, since expected payoff under 50/50 is the fair price.
The call is worth $10 because the stock can reach $110.
The call is worth $0 because the down move wipes out the payoff.
scenarios.why: The colleague priced under the real-world measure; arbitrage-free pricing uses the risk-neutral probability that makes the stock's expected growth equal the risk-free rate: p = (R*S − S_down)/(S_up − S_down) = (105 − 90)/20 = 0.75. Then V = (p*10 + (1−p)*0)/1.05 = 7.5/1.05 ≈ $7.14. This is exactly the cost of the replicating portfolio (delta = (10−0)/(110−90) = 0.5 shares), which is why no arbitrage is possible at any other price.
scenarios.hint: What probability makes the stock's expected one-period return exactly the risk-free rate?

domains.name: Start Here
domains.description: Orientation: how to use this bootcamp, math study strategy, the roadmap, and the computational lab setup.

scenarios.title: The Vague Theorem
scenarios.situation: A student 'knows' the central limit theorem but can't state the conditions (iid? finite variance? identical distribution?). They apply it to autocorrelated returns.
scenarios.prompt: What is the failure, and the fix?
choices: Definitions before theorems: the student memorized the conclusion without the hypotheses — so they can't check applicability. The fix is the definition-first habit: state conditions precisely, then verify them for the application (autocorrelated returns violate independence → CLT needs a dependent version or different tools). Vague hypotheses, misapplied theorems.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The pattern: conclusion-memorization without hypothesis-mastery. Every misapplied theorem in quant is this — the conditions are the applicability check, and skipping them is how models break silently. The definition-first habit (state it precisely, check it for the case) is the single highest-leverage study change.
scenarios.hint: What part of the theorem did the student skip?
evidence: Conclusions without conditions misapply. State, then check.

scenarios.title: The Read Proof
scenarios.situation: A student reads the proof of the tower property, follows each step, and nods. A week later they can't reproduce it.
scenarios.prompt: What happened, and what works instead?
choices: Fluency illusion: following a proof is recognition; reproducing it is recall — different cognitive processes. What works: close the book and re-derive (the key step: partition + linearity), fail, peek at one step, repeat. Proof reproduction with spaced retries builds the actual skill. Reading proofs is entertainment; reproducing them is training.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. The re-derive protocol: attempt from memory, note where you stall, peek minimally, retry. The stall points ARE the learning — they mark exactly what isn't owned. Three spaced reproductions beat ten readings. This applies to every proof in the bootcamp: tower property, Itô, CLT sketch, Black-Scholes.
scenarios.hint: Recognition or recall — which does reproducing test?
evidence: Close the book. Stall points mark what's unowned.

scenarios.title: The Unchecked Algebra
scenarios.situation: A student derives the Black-Scholes d1 by hand, makes a sign error, and never notices — the 'formula' is wrong for a week.
scenarios.prompt: What practice would have caught it instantly?
choices: Computational verification: plug the hand derivation into sympy/numpy and test against the known value (10.4506) — the sign error fails the check in seconds. The two-path standard: hand derivation + machine verification, independently. Algebra slips are inevitable; uncaught ones are a process failure. The computer is the proofreader.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. The known-value test (10.4506 for the canonical call) is the tripwire: any derivation error breaks it. This generalizes — every closed form in the bootcamp has a testable value. The discipline: never trust a hand derivation until the machine confirms it; never trust the machine until the hand understands it. Two paths, one answer.
scenarios.hint: What is the tripwire for derivation errors?
evidence: Hand derives; machine checks. 10.4506 is the tripwire.

scenarios.title: The Rush to Measure Theory
scenarios.situation: A student jumps to measure-theoretic probability in week 2 — sigma-algebras feel like alphabet soup, and they quit.
choices: Maturity ordering: measure theory compresses analysis (limits, continuity, convergence) into abstraction — without the concrete experience, the abstraction has nothing to attach to. The roadmap orders it at rung 8 deliberately: after analysis maturity. The fix isn't less ability, it's right sequencing — do calculus-analysis properly, and sigma-algebras become 'the thing we were doing all along, named.'
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. The abstraction ladder: concrete (calculus computations) → rigorous (analysis proofs) → abstract (measure theory). Each rung gives the next its meaning — skipping rungs gives symbols without referents. This is general: whenever mathematics feels like 'alphabet soup,' the fix is usually to descend to the concrete rung and climb again. Sequencing is pedagogy, not gatekeeping.
scenarios.hint: What does the abstraction attach to?
evidence: Abstraction needs concrete experience. Descend, then re-climb.

domains.name: Capstone: A Mathematical Pricing Library
domains.description: Build a derivatives pricing library from mathematical first principles: AD, Taylor, finite-difference PDEs, and convergence analysis.

scenarios.title: Why Dual Numbers?
scenarios.situation: A teammate says: 'just use finite differences for Greeks — simpler.' You're building the AD module anyway.
choices: Exactness: dual numbers give derivatives to machine precision — no step-size dilemma (too big: truncation error; too small: cancellation). Finite differences always trade the two; AD has neither. For Greeks (which feed hedging), the exactness matters — and the implementation teaches the chain rule as algebra. Simpler to write, harder to get right; AD is harder to write, impossible to get wrong.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. The step-size dilemma is fundamental: FD error = truncation (h²) + cancellation (eps/h) — no h is optimal in general. AD sidesteps it entirely via ε²=0 algebra. The pedagogical bonus: implementing AD makes the chain rule concrete (every op carries its derivative). For the capstone, exact Greeks validated to 1e-12 vs closed forms is the credibility.
scenarios.hint: What dilemma does finite differencing face?
evidence: AD: no step-size dilemma. Greeks to machine precision.

scenarios.title: The Exploding Grid
scenarios.situation: Your explicit FD solver produces option prices of 1e300. The code 'runs fine.'
scenarios.prompt: What happened, and why is the demo valuable?
choices: CFL violation: explicit schemes are conditionally stable — Δt beyond the limit amplifies errors exponentially (1e300 is the signature). The demo's value: stability isn't theoretical — it's the difference between a pricer and a random-number generator. The fix (smaller Δt or implicit scheme) teaches what the stability analysis predicts. Every PDE practitioner has seen 1e300; now you have too.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. The 1e300 signature is unmistakable: exponential error growth from violating the CFL condition. The demo converts the stability theorem from a formula into an experience — you'll never trust an explicit scheme without checking CFL again. The deeper lesson: numerical methods have contracts (stability conditions); violating them produces plausible-looking garbage, not errors.
scenarios.hint: What does 1e300 signify?
evidence: CFL violation → 1e300. Stability is the pricer.

scenarios.title: The Wrong Slope
scenarios.situation: Your convergence study shows slope 1.1 on log-log error vs dx. Theory says 2.0.
choices: A bug: the measured rate falsifies the implementation — something is first-order (a boundary condition, the American constraint, an upwinded term) or just wrong. The table did its job: it caught what unit tests missed. Debug by refining components separately (is the interior second-order? the boundary?). The convergence study is the implementation's lie detector.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. The rate IS the test: second-order theory + first-order measurement = first-order bug somewhere. Common culprits: boundary treatment, non-smooth payoffs (the kink at strike reduces observed order — expected and explainable), American constraint. The point: the table forces the investigation — 'close enough' thinking ships the bug. Measured rates are the numerical analyst's proof.
scenarios.hint: What is the convergence study actually testing?
evidence: Measured ≠ theory → bug. The table is the lie detector.

scenarios.title: Four Methods, One Truth
scenarios.situation: Why build four pricers (closed-form, tree, MC, PDE) for the same vanilla option? Isn't one enough?
choices: Cross-validation by construction: four independent implementations agreeing to tolerance is vastly stronger evidence than one implementation agreeing with itself. Each method has different bugs (PDE: stability; MC: scaling; tree: parameterization) — agreement means none of them bit. This is the scientific method applied to code: independent replication. One pricer is a claim; four agreeing pricers are a result.
Each is needed for different products.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The independence argument: the methods share only the mathematics — their implementations, failure modes, and approximations differ completely. Correlated bugs (same wrong formula copied) wouldn't survive; independent agreement is the gold standard. This is also the interview story: 'how do you know it's right?' → 'four independent methods agree, with measured convergence rates.'
scenarios.hint: What does agreement among independent methods prove?
evidence: Four methods agreeing > one method tested. Bugs differ; truth doesn't.

scenarios.title: The Scope Temptation
scenarios.situation: Week 4: you're tempted to add stochastic vol (Heston) to the library. The BS PDE solver isn't validated yet.
choices: Finish the foundation: an unvalidated BS solver plus Heston is two unvalidated solvers — complexity without credibility. The capstone's thesis is validation depth, not model breadth. Park Heston in 'future work' with the extension sketched (the PDE gains a dimension; the AD extends naturally). Interviewers probe what you BUILT deeply; Heston-as-bullet-point collapses under one question.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. The validation-depth thesis: the capstone differentiates on measured convergence rates and four-method agreement — both require finished, tested components. Heston doubles the work and halves the validation. The 'future work' sketch shows you know what's next without sacrificing what's now. Depth is graded; breadth is skimmed.
scenarios.hint: What is the capstone's actual thesis?
evidence: Depth is the differentiator. Future-work the rest.

domains.name: Linear Algebra
domains.description: Vector spaces, eigenvalues, decompositions, and projections — the linear algebra quants compute with daily.

scenarios.title: The Singular System
scenarios.situation: Ax = b with singular A. A junior says 'no solution.'
scenarios.prompt: When is the junior right, and what is the complete answer?
choices: Solvable iff b ∈ col(A) (b ⊥ null(A')) — then infinitely many solutions (particular + null(A)). If b ∉ col(A): no exact solution; the least-squares x = A⁺b minimizes ||Ax-b||. The junior is right only for inconsistent systems; the complete answer is the Fredholm alternative: solvable ⟺ b orthogonal to left null space. The pseudoinverse handles all cases uniformly.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. The Fredholm alternative is the complete picture: existence ⟺ b ∈ col(A) ⟺ b ⊥ ker(A'). The four subspaces (column, row, null, left-null) organize everything. In practice: np.linalg.lstsq returns the minimum-norm least-squares solution regardless — but knowing WHICH case you're in determines whether the answer is exact, approximate, or non-unique.
scenarios.hint: What must b satisfy for a solution to exist?
evidence: Fredholm alternative. Pseudoinverse unifies the cases.

scenarios.title: The Cholesky Failure
scenarios.situation: Cholesky on a covariance matrix fails. The matrix 'should' be PSD.
scenarios.prompt: What are the causes, and the fixes?
choices: Causes: rounding (near-singular → tiny negative eigenvalues), asynchronous data (pairwise covariances from different samples — not jointly PSD!), or genuine indefiniteness (bad estimate). Fixes: eigenvalue clipping (floor at small positive), shrinkage (Ledoit-Wolf toward diagonal — always PSD), or Higham's nearest-correlation-matrix. The failure is diagnostic — it caught a bad matrix before it poisoned the simulation.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. The pairwise-covariance trap is the classic: each pair estimated well, but the assembled matrix isn't PSD (no joint distribution has those marginals). Shrinkage fixes it structurally (convex combination with identity is always PSD). The lesson: Cholesky's failure is a FEATURE — it's the PSD test. Never bypass it; fix the matrix.
scenarios.hint: Why would 'good' pairwise estimates assemble badly?
evidence: Pairwise ≠ jointly PSD. Shrink; don't bypass.

scenarios.title: The 95% Variance
scenarios.situation: PCA keeps components explaining 95% of variance. A quant worries the discarded 5% holds the alpha.
choices: Sometimes: PCA maximizes VARIANCE explained, not signal — the alpha may live in low-variance directions (the discarded 5%). PCA is unsupervised: it doesn't know the target. For prediction, use supervised reduction (PLS, or just regularized regression on all features). Variance ≠ information; the worry is valid whenever signal concentrates in small-variance directions (common in finance: the 'surprise' is small but tradeable).
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The unsupervised trap: PCA optimizes reconstruction, not prediction — the discarded components are small-variance, not necessarily small-signal. In markets, the tradeable edge is often a small deviation (low variance, high information). The fix depends on the goal: compression → PCA; prediction → supervised methods. Know what your reduction optimizes.
scenarios.hint: What does PCA optimize — variance or signal?
evidence: PCA is unsupervised. Alpha may hide in the discarded 5%.

scenarios.title: The Ill-Conditioned Solve
scenarios.situation: Solving Ax=b, the answer changes wildly with tiny b perturbations. cond(A) = 1e12.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong, and what are the remedies?
choices: Ill-conditioning: relative error in x ≤ cond(A) × relative error in b — 1e12 amplifies rounding (1e-16) to O(1) garbage. The matrix is nearly singular. Remedies: regularization (ridge: (A'A+λI)^{-1}A'b), better formulation (avoid forming the ill-conditioned matrix), iterative refinement, or accept that the problem (not the algorithm) is hard — some systems are just sensitive. cond() diagnoses before you trust.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. The condition number is the sensitivity amplifier — it's a property of the PROBLEM, not the algorithm. No solver fixes 1e12 conditioning; regularization changes the problem to a nearby well-posed one (bias for stability — the bias-variance trade again). Always check cond() when solves look unstable; the number tells you whether to distrust the answer or reformulate.
scenarios.hint: Is conditioning about the algorithm or the problem?
evidence: Sensitivity is the problem's. Regularize or reformulate.

scenarios.title: The Rank-Deficient Regression
scenarios.situation: X'X is singular (perfect multicollinearity). The regression 'runs' but coefficients are garbage.
scenarios.prompt: What happened, and what is the principled fix?
choices: Non-identification: with rank-deficient X, infinitely many β give the same fit — the software picks one (min-norm via pseudoinverse) but it's meaningless. The principled fixes: drop/merge collinear features (substantive), regularize (ridge makes X'X+λI invertible — selects the min-norm-ish solution), or PCA regression. The garbage coefficients are all 'correct' (same fit!) — identification, not computation, failed.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. The identification failure: the DATA doesn't distinguish the solutions — no algorithm can. Ridge's fix is principled: among the infinite fits, prefer small coefficients (the bias-variance trade). Dropping features is substantive (which variable MEANS something?). The lesson: singular X'X is a data problem wearing a computation costume.
scenarios.hint: Can any algorithm fix non-identification?
evidence: Singular X'X = unidentified. Regularize or respecify.

scenarios.title: The Dominant Eigenvalue
scenarios.situation: You need only the largest eigenvalue of a 1M×1M sparse matrix. Full eigendecomposition is impossible.
choices: Power iteration: x_{k+1} = Ax_k/||Ax_k|| — converges to the dominant eigenvector (if |λ1|>|λ2|), eigenvalue via Rayleigh quotient. O(nnz) per iteration, matrix-free (only need matvecs). For the top-k: Lanczos/Arnoldi (scipy.sparse.linalg.eigsh). The lesson: match the algorithm to the need — full decompositions for small dense, iterative for large sparse. Never densify a sparse problem.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. The matrix-free principle: power iteration and Krylov methods only need A@v products — never the matrix itself. Convergence is geometric in |λ2/λ1| (slow if clustered — then use shifts). This is how Google's PageRank and large-scale PCA actually run. The algorithm follows the structure: sparse → iterative; dense small → direct.
scenarios.hint: What operation does power iteration actually need?
evidence: Power/Lanczos need only A@v. Never densify sparse.

scenarios.title: The Orthogonal Question
scenarios.situation: Why do numerical analysts love orthogonal matrices? What's special about Q'Q = I?
choices: (1) Norm-preserving: ||Qx|| = ||x|| — no amplification of errors. (2) Perfect conditioning: cond(Q) = 1 — solving with Q never blows up. (3) Trivial inverse: Q^{-1} = Q' — no factorization needed. Together: orthogonal transformations are the numerically safe operations — QR, SVD, and Householder reflections are all built on this. The love is earned: orthogonality is stability.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The three properties make orthogonal matrices the safe atoms of numerical linear algebra: they can't amplify errors (isometry), can't be ill-conditioned (cond 1), and invert for free. This is WHY QR beats normal equations, WHY SVD is the stable decomposition, WHY we orthogonalize. Design algorithms from orthogonal pieces and stability follows.
scenarios.hint: Which property prevents error amplification?
evidence: Isometry + cond 1 + free inverse. Build from orthogonal pieces.

domains.name: Calculus & Analysis
domains.description: Limits, Taylor's theorem, integration, multivariable calculus, and the rigor beneath the computations.

scenarios.title: The Flat Function
scenarios.situation: f(x) = e^{-1/x²} (f(0)=0) is infinitely differentiable, yet its Taylor series at 0 (all zeros) doesn't equal f anywhere except 0.
scenarios.prompt: What does this destroy, and what survives?
choices: It destroys 'smooth ⟹ analytic': infinite differentiability does NOT imply Taylor convergence to f — the remainder doesn't vanish. What survives: Taylor's theorem WITH remainder (still valid — the remainder accounts for the gap), and the lesson that approximation needs the remainder bound, not just smoothness. The flat function is why analysts always carry the remainder.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. The subtlety: Taylor's THEOREM (with remainder) holds perfectly — it's the informal 'Taylor series = function' that's false. The remainder R_n doesn't → 0 here (derivatives grow super-exponentially off 0). The practical lesson: in quant, Taylor approximations (Greeks! FD!) need remainder/error analysis — smoothness alone never justifies truncation.
scenarios.hint: Which is true: the theorem or the slogan?

scenarios.title: The Swapped Limit
scenarios.situation: A derivation swaps lim and ∫ without comment. The result is used in a pricing proof.
scenarios.prompt: When is this legal, and what is the risk?
choices: Legal under: uniform convergence (Weierstrass M-test), dominated convergence (integrable dominator — the probabilist's license), or monotone convergence (nonnegative increasing). The risk: without justification the swap can be FALSE (classic counterexamples: spikes sliding to infinity — mass escapes). In pricing: interchanging E and lim needs DCT usually — check the dominator (payoff bounds often provide it). Unjustified swaps are the most common analysis error.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The 'spike' counterexample: f_n = indicator of [n, n+1] — ∫f_n = 1 always, but f_n → 0 pointwise, ∫lim = 0 ≠ 1 = lim∫. Mass escapes to infinity; DCT's dominator prevents exactly this. In quant the payoff's integrability usually supplies the dominator — but you must CHECK. The checklist from the pitfalls lesson exists for this.
scenarios.hint: What prevents mass from escaping?
evidence: DCT/MCT/uniform. The spike counterexample is the warning.

scenarios.title: The Mean That Isn't
scenarios.situation: A model assumes stock returns have a finite mean. The returns look Cauchy-ish (heavy tails).
choices: The mean may not EXIST: Cauchy has undefined expectation (∫|x|f = ∞) — LLN fails, sample means don't converge (they're Cauchy-distributed themselves!), and every mean-based method (OLS! Sharpe!) is vacuous. What breaks: all of classical statistics' asymptotics. The fix: check tail integrability first; use medians/robust methods for heavy tails. The integral decides existence — not the notation E[X].
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. The sample mean of Cauchy data IS Cauchy (same distribution!) — averaging does nothing. This breaks LLN, CLT, and every downstream method silently. The quant relevance: financial returns have heavy tails (not Cauchy, but heavier than normal) — tail awareness isn't pedantry, it's the difference between methods that work and methods that assume. Check integrability; the integral is the existence proof.
scenarios.hint: What is the distribution of the Cauchy sample mean?
evidence: Cauchy mean: undefined. Sample mean: still Cauchy. Check integrability.

scenarios.title: The δ That Depends
scenarios.situation: f(x) = x² is continuous everywhere. Is it uniformly continuous on R? On [0,1]?
choices: On [0,1]: yes (Heine-Cantor: continuous on compact ⟹ uniform). On R: NO — the δ needed shrinks as x grows (|x²-y²| = |x-y||x+y|; for large x+y, tiny |x-y| still gives large difference). The distinction: uniform needs ONE δ for all x (∀ε∃δ∀x); ordinary allows δ(x) (∀x∀ε∃δ). The quantifier order IS the concept. Relevance: uniform convergence/continuity is what licenses interchanges.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. The computation: given ε, need |x-y| < ε/|x+y| — the required δ → 0 as x → ∞, so no single δ works on R. On [0,1], |x+y| ≤ 2, so δ = ε/2 works uniformly. This is the canonical example for the quantifier-order distinction — and it matters because uniform (not pointwise) is the interchange license.
scenarios.hint: Why does the required δ shrink with x?

scenarios.title: The IVP Without Uniqueness
scenarios.situation: y' = √|y|, y(0) = 0. A student applies an ODE solver and gets y = 0. Another gets y = x²/4.
choices: Both — non-uniqueness: √|y| isn't Lipschitz at 0 (derivative blows up), so Picard-Lindelöf doesn't apply; solutions include y=0, y=x²/4 (for x≥0), and spliced combinations (stay at 0 until a, then branch). The solver returned one valid solution silently. The lesson: existence/uniqueness needs Lipschitz (or Osgood); without it, numerics pick arbitrarily. Check conditions before computing.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. The Lipschitz failure at 0 (√|y| has infinite slope there) voids uniqueness — infinitely many solutions thread the initial point. The solver's silence is the danger: it returned A solution, not THE solution. In quant: SDE coefficients need Lipschitz for strong uniqueness — non-Lipschitz models (some stochastic vol!) have the same pathology. Conditions first, computation second.
scenarios.hint: What condition guarantees uniqueness, and does it hold here?

scenarios.title: The Double Sum
scenarios.situation: A derivation swaps Σ_n Σ_m for Σ_m Σ_n in an expectation computation. When is this valid?
choices: Tonelli (nonnegative terms: always swappable) or Fubini (absolutely summable: Σ|a_nm| < ∞). Without these, the swap can change the value (conditionally convergent double series — the discrete Riemann rearrangement). In expectation computations: E[ΣX_n] = ΣE[X_n] needs Tonelli (nonnegative) or DCT/uniform integrability. The justification is absolute summability — the discrete DCT.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The double-series version of the interchange problem: order of summation matters exactly when absolute convergence fails. Tonelli (nonnegative) is the free case — always valid. Fubini needs Σ|a| < ∞. In quant derivations (expanding payoffs, interchanging E and sums), the nonnegativity or integrability check is the license. Unjustified swaps are the analysis pitfall in series clothing.
scenarios.hint: What is the discrete version of DCT?
evidence: Tonelli/Fubini license the swap. Check first.

scenarios.title: The Implicit Function
scenarios.situation: An equation F(x,y) = 0 defines y as a function of x 'locally.' When does this work, and what is the derivative?
choices: Implicit function theorem: if F(a,b)=0 and ∂F/∂y(a,b) ≠ 0, then locally y = g(x) with g'(x) = -F_x/F_y. The non-vanishing partial is the condition — it's the local invertibility that makes y solvable. Use: comparative statics (how does the implied vol change with price? — differentiate the defining equation), constraint manifolds. The derivative formula is the total differential: F_x dx + F_y dy = 0.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. The condition ∂F/∂y ≠ 0 is the local solvability — where it vanishes, the curve may fold (no function). The derivative via total differential is the workhorse: for implied vol σ(S) defined by C_BS(σ) = C_market, dσ/dS = -(∂C/∂S)/(∂C/∂σ) = -Δ/ν — the skew's calculus! The IFT turns implicit definitions into differentiable functions.
scenarios.hint: How do you differentiate what you can't solve explicitly?
evidence: F_x dx + F_y dy = 0. IFT: the local license.

domains.name: Probability Theory
domains.description: Rigorous probability: axioms, random variables, expectation, conditioning, and the limit theorems with proofs.

scenarios.title: The Neither Distribution
scenarios.situation: A student claims every random variable is discrete or continuous. You mention the Cantor distribution.
scenarios.prompt: What is it, and why does it matter?
choices: The Cantor function (Devil's staircase): continuous, nondecreasing, constant on the Cantor set's complement, rising only on the null Cantor set — its 'density' would be 0 a.e. yet it rises from 0 to 1. No pmf (no atoms: continuous), no pdf (derivative 0 a.e.). It matters because: the discrete/continuous dichotomy is FALSE (Lebesgue decomposition: discrete + absolutely continuous + singular), and 'pathological' cases test whether definitions are complete. Rigor means covering all cases.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The Cantor distribution is singular continuous — the third Lebesgue component. Its existence proves the dichotomy false and motivates the measure-theoretic framework (which handles all three uniformly via dP). The practical moral: definitions must cover the weird cases — 'obvious' classifications often aren't exhaustive. This is why we do measure theory.
scenarios.hint: What are the three Lebesgue components?
evidence: Discrete + AC + singular. Rigor covers all cases.

scenarios.title: The Concave Utility
scenarios.situation: An investor with concave utility u is offered a fair gamble (E[gamble] = 0). What does Jensen say?
choices: No: E[u(w + gamble)] ≤ u(w + E[gamble]) = u(w) — the gamble reduces expected utility despite zero expected monetary value. Jensen's inequality IS risk aversion: concave utility ⟺ risk-averse. The risk premium (what they'd pay to avoid it) ≈ -½A·Var (Arrow-Pratt, via Taylor). This is the mathematical foundation of insurance, diversification, and every risk measure.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. The fair gamble's expected VALUE is zero but its expected UTILITY is negative — value ≠ utility is the entire point of Jensen here. The Arrow-Pratt approximation (risk premium ≈ ½·(absolute risk aversion)·variance) comes from Taylor-expanding u around w — Taylor and Jensen collaborating. Risk aversion isn't psychology; it's concavity.
scenarios.hint: What does concavity of u encode?
evidence: E[u] ≤ u(E). Fair gambles hurt. Arrow-Pratt quantifies.

scenarios.title: The Convergent That Isn't
scenarios.situation: X_n → X in distribution. A student concludes E[X_n] → E[X] and P(X_n → X) = 1.
choices: (1) Convergence in distribution doesn't imply moment convergence — need uniform integrability (mass can escape: X_n = n with prob 1/n). (2) It's the WEAKEST mode — no pathwise claim at all (Skorokhod representation gives a.s. convergence only on a reconstructed space). The hierarchy: a.s. ⟹ prob ⟹ dist. Each arrow is strict — counterexamples separate them. Know which mode your theorem gives.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. The escaping-mass counterexample (P(X_n=n)=1/n, else 0): X_n → 0 in prob (hence dist) but E[X_n] = 1 forever. Uniform integrability is the missing condition for moment convergence. The hierarchy's strictness is the lesson: stronger conclusions need stronger modes — check which the theorem actually provides before using the conclusion.
scenarios.hint: What is the weakest mode, and what does it not give?
evidence: dist < prob < a.s. Moments need UI. Check the mode.

scenarios.title: Infinitely Often
scenarios.situation: Events A_n with ΣP(A_n) = ∞, independent. What is P(A_n occurs infinitely often)?
scenarios.prompt: What does Borel-Cantelli say, and why does independence matter?
choices: P = 1 (second Borel-Cantelli): with independence and divergent sum, infinitely many occur a.s. Independence is ESSENTIAL — without it, the events could be nested decreasing (A_n ↓ with P(A_n) = 1/n: sum diverges but P(i.o.) = 0!). The first BC (convergent sum ⟹ P(i.o.)=0) needs no independence. The pair is the almost-sure workhorse: strong LLN, recurrence, and 'eventually always' arguments all run on BC.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. The nested counterexample shows why independence can't be dropped: A_n decreasing with P(A_n)=1/n has ΣP=∞ but ∩A_n has probability lim 1/n = 0 — finitely many occur a.s. The second BC's proof (via complements and 1-x ≤ e^{-x}) uses independence to factor. This lemma proves the strong LLN — it's not a curiosity, it's load-bearing.
scenarios.hint: Why can't independence be dropped?
evidence: Σ<∞ → 0 i.o. (no indep needed). Σ=∞ + indep → 1 i.o.

scenarios.title: The Pricing Tower
scenarios.situation: Price a derivative paying X_T by iterated conditioning: E_Q[e^{-rT}X_T] = E_Q[E_Q[e^{-rT}X_T | F_t]].
scenarios.prompt: Why is the tower the pricing workhorse?
choices: It justifies backward induction: price = conditional expectation given today's information of the conditional expectation given tomorrow's — the tower collapses nested conditionings. Binomial trees ARE the tower (condition on each node's information, collapse backward). Dynamic programming, Bellman equations, American option backward induction — all tower applications. The tower turns 'condition on everything' into 'condition stepwise.'
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The binomial tree's backward induction is literally E_Q[·|F_0] = E_Q[E_Q[·|F_1]|F_0] = ... — each step conditions on finer information, and the tower guarantees the collapse. American pricing (Snell envelope: V_t = max(exercise, E[V_{t+1}|F_t])) is the tower with optimal stopping. The tower isn't notation — it's the computational strategy for every multi-period price.
scenarios.hint: What is backward induction, really?
evidence: Trees, Bellman, Snell — all tower applications.

scenarios.title: The Fourier of Probability
scenarios.situation: Why prove the CLT with characteristic functions instead of directly with CDFs?
choices: Algebraization: φ_{X+Y} = φ_X·φ_Y (independence → multiplication) — convolution becomes pointwise multiplication, and the CLT's √n scaling becomes φ(t/√n)^n → e^{-t²/2} via log-Taylor. Direct CDF work with convolutions is intractable; Fourier transforms linearize the operation. Plus: φ determines the law uniquely (inversion/uniqueness theorems). The technique generalizes: characteristic functions are THE tool for sums of independents.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. The key computation: log φ(t/√n) = -σ²t²/(2n) + o(1/n) (Taylor of φ at 0, using φ(0)=1, φ'(0)=iμ, φ''(0)=-E[X²]) — then n·log → -σ²t²/2. Lévy's continuity theorem closes: pointwise φ convergence ⟹ distribution convergence. This is the standard CLT proof — and the template for every 'sums converge' argument in probability.
scenarios.hint: What does independence become under φ?
evidence: φ turns sums into products. The CLT's engine.

scenarios.title: The Coupling Proof
scenarios.situation: To bound the distance between two distributions, a probabilist constructs them on the SAME probability space (coupling).
scenarios.prompt: What is the idea, and what does it prove easily?
choices: Coupling: build X~μ, Y~ν jointly to make them EQUAL with high probability — then total variation d(μ,ν) ≤ P(X≠Y) (coupling inequality). It proves convergence bounds cleanly: MCMC mixing (couple two chains, bound meeting time), Poisson approximation (Stein's method is coupling-adjacent). The idea: distance between LAWS via construction of joint REALIZATIONS. Existence of good couplings ⟹ closeness of distributions.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. The coupling inequality is the payoff: d_TV ≤ P(X≠Y) — bound the meeting probability, bound the distributional distance. For MCMC: couple a chain from stationarity with one from arbitrary start; when they meet, they've mixed — mixing time ≤ coupling time. The method turns analytic distance questions into probabilistic construction questions, which are often easier. A core modern technique.
scenarios.hint: How does coupling bound distributional distance?

domains.name: Statistical Methods
domains.description: Estimation theory, testing, regression, and Bayesian inference — statistics with mathematical teeth.

scenarios.title: The Sufficient Statistic
scenarios.situation: For X_i ~ N(θ,1), is the sample mean sufficient? The sample median?
scenarios.prompt: What does sufficiency mean here, and why does it matter?
choices: Mean: YES (factorization: the likelihood depends on data only through x̄ — exponential family). Median: NO (loses information about θ beyond x̄). It matters via Rao-Blackwell: any unbiased estimator conditioned on x̄ improves (or ties) — the mean is already the UMVUE here. Sufficiency is data compression without information loss: x̄ carries ALL the sample's information about θ. The median discards some.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. The factorization check: L(θ) = (2π)^{-n/2}exp(-Σ(x_i-θ)²/2) — Σ(x_i-θ)² = Σ(x_i-x̄)² + n(x̄-θ)², so L factors through x̄. The median can't achieve this (the likelihood needs more than the median). Rao-Blackwell then says: condition anything on x̄. Sufficiency is the information-theoretic compression — keep the sufficient statistic, discard the rest.
scenarios.hint: What does the likelihood factor through?
evidence: Sufficient stats carry all information. Rao-Blackwell the rest.

scenarios.title: The Most Powerful Test
scenarios.situation: Testing H0: θ=0 vs H1: θ=1 (simple vs simple, normal data). What is the optimal test?
choices: Reject for large likelihood ratio L = f1(x)/f0(x) — for normal with known variance, this reduces to rejecting for large x̄ (the ratio is monotone in x̄). NP says: among ALL level-α tests, the LR test maximizes power — no test does better. The prescription is exact (not asymptotic) for simple-vs-simple. For composite alternatives, MLR families (Karlin-Rubin) extend it; otherwise UMP may not exist.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. The LR computation: log L = Σ[(x_i-1)² - x_i²]/(-2)... = n·x̄ - n/2 (for unit variance) — monotone increasing in x̄, so 'large L' ⟺ 'large x̄'. NP's optimality is the gold standard: it defines what 'best test' MEANS (max power at given size). The limitation: simple-vs-simple only — composite hypotheses need more (GLRT + Wilks, asymptotically).
scenarios.hint: What is the LR monotone in?
evidence: Simple-vs-simple: reject for large f1/f0. Max power, exact.

scenarios.title: The Halved Slope
scenarios.situation: A regression of y on a noisy-measured x gives slope 1.0. The measurement error variance equals the true x variance. What is the true slope?
choices: 2.0: attenuation factor = Var(x*)/(Var(x*)+σ²_u) = 1/2 — the observed slope is half the true. True = observed/factor = 1.0/0.5 = 2.0. The correction needs the noise variance (from validation data or instruments). Without it, the slope is biased toward zero — ALWAYS (single regressor). This is why 'insignificant' factors with noisy measurement may be important.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. The attenuation formula plim(β̂) = β·σ²_x*/(σ²_x*+σ²_u) — with equal variances, the factor is exactly 1/2. The correction divides by the factor — but the factor needs the measurement-error variance, which the data alone doesn't identify (need replicates, validation, or instruments). The quant lesson: noisy regressors understate effects; 'no effect found' may mean 'noisy measurement.'
scenarios.hint: What identifies the correction factor?

scenarios.title: The Vanishing Prior
scenarios.situation: With n=1,000,000, a Bayesian and frequentist report identical intervals. With n=10, they differ sharply.
choices: Bernstein-von Mises: the posterior converges to N(θ̂_MLE, I^{-1}/n) — the prior's influence decays as 1/n while the likelihood's grows as n. At n=10⁶ the prior is 4 pseudo-observations against a million — invisible. At n=10, the prior is 30% of the information — decisive. The theorem reconciles the philosophies asymptotically AND quantifies when they differ: small data is where priors matter, which is exactly where you need them most.
n=10 is too small for any inference.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The 1/n vs n scaling is the mechanism: posterior ≈ likelihood × prior, and the likelihood concentrates at rate n while the prior stays fixed. The practical import: with big data, just be Bayesian or frequentist (same answer); with small data, the prior IS the analysis — choose it carefully and report sensitivity. The theorem tells you which regime you're in.
scenarios.hint: At what n does the prior stop mattering?
evidence: Big n: philosophies agree. Small n: prior is decisive.

scenarios.title: The Bootstrap That Lied
scenarios.situation: Bootstrapping the sample maximum to get its CI. The intervals are too narrow and miss the truth.
scenarios.prompt: Why does the bootstrap fail here?
choices: Non-smoothness: the maximum is a non-differentiable functional — the bootstrap's consistency needs smoothness (Hadamard differentiability). The bootstrap max of resamples can't exceed the sample max (support truncation!) — the resampled maxima pile at the observed max, understating uncertainty. The fix: parametric bootstrap (assume the tail model), or extreme-value theory directly. Bootstrap is not magic — it needs the statistic to be smooth enough.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. The support mechanism: resampling from {x_1..x_n}, the max is ≤ observed max ALWAYS — the bootstrap distribution is truncated at the very quantity being estimated. For smooth statistics (means, medians, regression coefficients) the bootstrap's Edgeworth-level accuracy is excellent; for extremes it fails structurally. Know the boundary: smooth functionals ✓, extremes/superefficient ✗.
scenarios.hint: What can't the resampled max exceed?
evidence: Max: resamples ≤ observed max. Use EVT instead.

scenarios.title: The Wrong Standard Errors
scenarios.situation: OLS coefficients look right, but the model is misspecified (nonlinearity). The usual SEs are wrong.
choices: Sandwich (robust) variance: (X'X)^{-1}(X'Ω̂X)(X'X)^{-1} — consistent for the true sampling variance even under misspecification (White). The 'bread' is the model-based variance; the 'meat' estimates the actual score variance. Under correct specification it reduces to the usual; under misspecification it stays honest. The lesson: the point estimate may survive misspecification, but the SEs need the sandwich. Huber-White or bust.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. The sandwich's robustness: it estimates Var(score) empirically rather than assuming the model's information equality — so heteroskedasticity, mild misspecification, and clustering don't break it. M-estimation theory generalizes: every estimator has a sandwich variance. The quant practice: clustered/robust SEs by default — the model is always slightly wrong; the SEs shouldn't be.
scenarios.hint: What does the 'meat' estimate?

scenarios.title: The 1000 Tests
scenarios.situation: Testing 1000 strategies, you want to control false discoveries but Bonferroni kills all power.
choices: Benjamini-Hochberg FDR: control the EXPECTED PROPORTION of false discoveries (not the probability of any) — sort p-values, find the largest k with p_(k) ≤ (k/m)α, reject the top k. Far more powerful than Bonferroni when many true effects exist; the discoveries are 'mostly true' (FDR ≤ α). The error-rate choice: FWER (Bonferroni) for confirmatory (drug trials), FDR for exploratory (strategy mining). Match the rate to the goal.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. The FDR/FWER distinction: FWER controls P(any false positive) — draconian with 1000 tests; FDR controls E[false/rejected] — allows some false positives among many discoveries. BH's procedure is simple and valid under independence (or positive dependence). For quant research (exploratory, many candidates), FDR is the standard; for the final 'ship it' test, FWER. The error rate is a choice, not a default.
scenarios.hint: FWER or FDR — when each?
evidence: FDR for discovery, FWER for confirmation. BH procedure.

domains.name: Optimization Methods
domains.description: Convexity, gradient methods, Lagrange duality, and the optimization powering model fitting and portfolios.

scenarios.title: The Certificate
scenarios.situation: You minimized a convex function and found ∇f = 0. Is it the global min?
choices: Yes — convexity's certificate: for convex f, any stationary point is a global minimizer (proof: f(y) ≥ f(x) + ∇f(x)'(y-x) = f(x)). No other class offers this — it's THE reason convex optimization is tractable. The certificate is the convexity proof (Hessian ⪰ 0, or composition rules), not the gradient alone. Non-convex: ∇f=0 could be a saddle or local min — no certificate.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. The first-order inequality f(y) ≥ f(x)+∇f(x)'(y-x) IS convexity's definition in differentiable form — at ∇f(x)=0 it gives f(y) ≥ f(x) for all y. The workflow: prove convex (Hessian/composition), find stationary point, done — certified global. This is why convex problems are 'solved' and non-convex are 'attempted.'
scenarios.hint: What makes ∇f=0 sufficient here?
evidence: Stationary + convex = global min. Prove convex first.

scenarios.title: The Diverging Descent
scenarios.situation: Gradient descent on a smooth convex f diverges. α was 'small' (0.1).
choices: α > 2/L: 'small' is relative — stability needs α ≤ 1/L (L = gradient Lipschitz constant). If L = 100, α=0.1 diverges (0.1 > 0.02). The fix: backtracking line search (adapts to the local L) or estimate L (λ_max of Hessian). 'Small' without reference to L is meaningless — the step must be small RELATIVE TO the curvature. This is the #1 GD bug.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. The stability boundary α < 2/L is sharp: beyond it, the iterates oscillate and explode (the quadratic case shows this exactly: x_{k+1} = (1-αλ)x_k diverges for αλ > 2). Backtracking removes the guesswork: shrink α until Armijo's sufficient-decrease holds. The lesson: steps are measured against curvature, not against intuition.
scenarios.hint: Small relative to what?

scenarios.title: The Inactive Constraint
scenarios.situation: At the optimum, g_1(x*) < 0 (strictly satisfied). What is λ_1?
choices: λ_1 = 0 by complementary slackness (λ_i·g_i = 0): the constraint doesn't bind, so its shadow price is zero — tightening/relaxing it doesn't change the optimum. The economics: non-binding constraints are free. The KKT system uses this to identify the active set: solve assuming a set binds, verify λ ≥ 0 and feasibility. Complementary slackness is the on/off switch of constraints.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Complementary slackness forces the dichotomy: g_i < 0 ⟹ λ_i = 0; λ_i > 0 ⟹ g_i = 0. The active-set strategy exploits this: guess which constraints bind, solve the equality problem, check the guess (λ ≥ 0 for assumed-active, g ≤ 0 for assumed-inactive). It's the combinatorial heart of constrained optimization — which constraints matter is the discrete decision.
scenarios.hint: What does λ_i = 0 mean economically?
evidence: Inactive ⟹ λ=0. The constraint is free.

scenarios.title: Newton Gone Wild
scenarios.situation: Newton's method from a far starting point diverges — the Hessian isn't positive definite there.
choices: Damped Newton (line search on the Newton direction — the direction may still be good), trust regions (limit the step to where the quadratic model is trusted), or Levenberg-Marquardt (H + μI — force positive definiteness; μ→0 near solution recovers quadratic convergence). Pure Newton is only locally convergent — globalization (line search/trust region) makes it practical. The Hessian's indefiniteness far away is expected, not a bug.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. The locality issue: Newton's quadratic model is only valid near x* — far away, H may be indefinite and the 'Newton step' points anywhere. Trust regions formalize 'where the model is trusted' (adjust radius by agreement); damping just shortens the step. LM's μI interpolation (gradient-like far, Newton-like near) is the standard compromise. Globalization + fast local convergence = practical Newton.
scenarios.hint: Why does pure Newton only work locally?
evidence: Line search/trust region/LM. Quadratic model is local.

scenarios.title: The Noisy Gradient
scenarios.situation: SGD with constant step size oscillates around the optimum but never converges.
choices: Robbins-Monro: need Σα_k = ∞ (reach everywhere) and Σα_k² < ∞ (noise dies) — constant α violates the second; the noise never decays. Fix: decaying schedule (α_k = α_0/(1+γk), or step decay), or averaging (Polyak-Ruppert: average the iterates — optimal asymptotic rate even with constant-ish steps). The oscillation IS the theory: constant steps + persistent noise = stationary distribution around x*, not convergence.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. The two conditions are intuitive: Σα=∞ (infinite total travel — can reach the optimum from anywhere), Σα²<∞ (finite total noise variance — the jitter dies). Constant α gives infinite noise energy — the iterates converge IN DISTRIBUTION to a neighborhood, not to the point. Schedules (1/k, cosine, step decay) or iterate averaging resolve it. The oscillation's SIZE (~α·noise) even diagnoses the step.
scenarios.hint: What do the two Robbins-Monro conditions mean?
evidence: Σα=∞ reach; Σα²<∞ quiet. Or Polyak-average.

scenarios.title: The Positive Gap
scenarios.situation: You compute primal value 5.0, dual value 4.2. The problem is non-convex.
scenarios.prompt: What does the gap tell you?
choices: The duality gap (0.8) bounds suboptimality: f* ≥ 4.2 (dual is a lower bound even without strong duality — weak duality always holds). The gap measures non-convexity's cost: the dual can't see the non-convex structure. Use: branch-and-bound (gap drives the search), convex relaxations (minimize the gap), or accept 4.2 as the certificate of 'no better than.' The gap is information, not failure.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. Weak duality's universality: g(λ) ≤ f* for ANY problem — the dual always certifies a lower bound. The gap's size quantifies how much the non-convexity costs (convex ⟹ gap closable via Slater). In global optimization, the gap IS the progress metric: branch-and-bound terminates when gap < tolerance. Don't mourn the gap — use it.
scenarios.hint: What does weak duality guarantee, even here?
evidence: Dual ≤ primal always. Gap bounds suboptimality.

scenarios.title: The 1e6 Variable
scenarios.situation: min f(x1,x2) with x1 ~ 1e6, x2 ~ 1e-6 scale. Every optimizer struggles.
choices: Rescale: z1 = x1/1e6, z2 = x2/1e-6 — optimize in z (all O(1)), transform back. The Hessian's eigenvalues span 12 orders of magnitude unscaled (κ ~ 1e12) — no algorithm survives that; scaled, κ ~ O(1) and everything converges. This is THE highest-ROI practical trick: precondition by diagonal scaling. Automatic in good software (often); manual when not. Diagnose: print variable scales before optimizing.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The conditioning argument: the Hessian in x-coordinates has eigenvalues differing by ~1e12 — GD's rate (1-μ/L) ≈ 1-1e-12 (frozen), Newton's H is numerically singular. Diagonal scaling is the universal preconditioner: z = D^{-1}x makes the problem isotropic-ish. The rule: all optimization variables should be O(1) — scale first, optimize second, always.
scenarios.hint: Why does scale destroy conditioning?
evidence: κ ~ 1e12 unscaled. Diagonal scaling is the free fix.

domains.name: Differential Equations
domains.description: ODEs, the heat equation, Black-Scholes PDE, and Feynman-Kac — dynamics made rigorous.

scenarios.title: The Non-Lipschitz ODE
scenarios.situation: y' = √|y|, y(0) = 0 — how many solutions?
scenarios.prompt: What does Picard-Lindelöf say, and what are the solutions?
choices: Infinitely many: y ≡ 0, y = x²/4 (x≥0), and splices (0 until a, then (x-a)²/4). Picard-Lindelöf needs Lipschitz f in y — √|y| has infinite slope at 0, so no uniqueness guarantee. The theorem's condition is sharp: without Lipschitz, uniqueness genuinely fails (not just unproven). The numerical warning: solvers return ONE solution silently — which one depends on the method. Always check Lipschitz before trusting ODE numerics.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. The splice construction: stay at 0 for x ∈ [0,a], then follow (x-a)²/4 — each a gives a valid C¹ solution. The Lipschitz condition isn't technical fussiness; it's the exact boundary of uniqueness. In SDEs, the same issue (non-Lipschitz coefficients) breaks strong uniqueness — some stochastic vol models live here. Conditions aren't suggestions.
scenarios.hint: Where does Lipschitz fail, and why does it matter?
evidence: √|y| not Lipschitz at 0 → infinite solutions. Check first.

scenarios.title: The Interior Peak
scenarios.situation: A numerical heat-equation solution shows an interior maximum growing in time. The initial data had max 1.0; now it's 1.5.
scenarios.prompt: What does the maximum principle say?
choices: Impossible for the true solution: without sources, interior maxima can't exceed boundary/initial data (max ≤ 1.0 always). The 1.5 is NUMERICAL — instability (CFL violated) or a boundary-condition bug. The maximum principle is the PDE's built-in validator: violations diagnose the scheme, not the physics. Trust the theorem over the numbers; fix the scheme.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The strong maximum principle: non-constant solutions can't attain interior maxima — the peak must live on the parabolic boundary (initial time or spatial boundary). A growing interior peak is the numerical scheme's confession. This is qualitative validation: before checking numbers, check properties (maxima, positivity, conservation) — theorems as debuggers.
scenarios.hint: What is the scheme confessing?
evidence: Interior growth ⟹ scheme bug. Qualitative checks first.

scenarios.title: The Heat in Disguise
scenarios.situation: The Black-Scholes PDE looks nothing like the heat equation. Yet they're equivalent.
scenarios.prompt: What is the transformation, and why does it matter?
choices: x = ln(S/K), τ = T - t, V(S,t) = K·e^{-rτ}·u(x,τ) (plus drift adjustments) — the log transform kills the S² and S coefficients (constant-coefficient PDE!), time reversal fixes the direction, discounting removes -rV. Result: ∂u/∂τ = ½σ²∂²u/∂x² — the heat equation. It matters because: the BS closed form IS the heat kernel (that's why N(d) appears — it's the normal CDF!), and every heat-equation result (maximum principle, fundamental solution) transfers to BS.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. The N(d1), N(d2) in Black-Scholes are normal CDFs because the solution is a heat kernel (Gaussian) — the formula's shape was inevitable once the PDE became the heat equation. The transform also explains the lognormal: x = ln S diffuses normally, so S is lognormal. PDE transformations aren't tricks — they reveal what the equation IS.
scenarios.hint: Why does the normal CDF appear in Black-Scholes?
evidence: Log transform → heat equation → Gaussian → N(d). Inevitable.

scenarios.title: The Free Boundary
scenarios.situation: Pricing an American put by PDE: where is the difficulty beyond the European case?
choices: The optimal exercise boundary S*(t): below it, exercise (V = K-S); above it, hold (PDE holds). The boundary is UNKNOWN — part of the solution (it's where value-matching AND smooth-pasting hold: V and V' continuous). This makes it a free-boundary problem: the domain itself is solved for. Methods: front-fixing (change variables to fix it), penalty (soften the constraint), PSOR. The boundary's shape (S*(t) increasing in t) is the economics: exercise region grows as expiry nears.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. The complementarity system: V ≥ payoff, PDE-residual ≤ 0, product = 0 — at each (S,t), either you hold (PDE) or exercise (value = intrinsic). Smooth pasting (V' continuous at S*) is the optimality condition — it's what SELECTS the boundary. The economics: S*(t) rises toward K as t→T (less time value to protect). Free boundaries are the hard part of American pricing in every method (trees handle it naturally — that's their edge).
scenarios.hint: What two conditions hold at S*(t)?

scenarios.title: Which Side?
scenarios.situation: You can price by PDE (finite differences) or by expectation (Monte Carlo). Feynman-Kac says both work.
choices: By dimension and path-dependence: low-D European/American → PDE/FD (fast, Greeks free via the grid); high-D or path-dependent → MC (dimension-independent, path features free). Americans in high-D → LSM (the hybrid). The choice is computational, not philosophical — Feynman-Kac guarantees the same answer; the methods differ in cost. The quant's skill: match the method to the problem's structure (the PDE-vs-MC decision from the ladder, now theorem-backed).
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. The decision matrix: FD wins low-D (grids feasible, Greeks by differentiation, American via complementarity); MC wins high-D/path-dependent (no grid, payoffs from paths). Feynman-Kac is the guarantee that the choice is about cost, not correctness. Wrong choice = 100x slower or infeasible — the most expensive mistake is methodological, not implementational.
scenarios.hint: What does Feynman-Kac guarantee about the choice?
evidence: FK: same answer. Choose by dimension/path-dependence.

scenarios.title: Read the Generator
scenarios.situation: dX = κ(θ-X)dt + σdW (Ornstein-Uhlenbeck). What is its generator, and what does it tell you?
choices: Lf = κ(θ-x)f' + ½σ²f'' — the expected instantaneous rate of change of f(X_t). It tells you: the PDE for E[g(X_T)] (Feynman-Kac: ∂u/∂t + Lu = 0), the stationary distribution (solve L*π = 0 — the adjoint!), and long-run behavior. For OU: stationary is N(θ, σ²/2κ) — the mean-reversion's equilibrium. The generator is the process's DNA: everything (PDE, stationary, expectations) unfolds from L.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The stationary check: L* (adjoint) π = 0 with π = N(θ, σ²/2κ) — verify by differentiation. The generator's power: it's the single object from which the PDE (Feynman-Kac), the stationary law (adjoint), and the martingale problem all flow. 'Read the generator' means: given an SDE, immediately write L — it's the first step of every analysis.
scenarios.hint: What flows from L?
evidence: PDE, stationary, expectations — all from the generator.

scenarios.title: The Wrong Boundary
scenarios.situation: Your FD pricer uses V(S_max) = 0 for a call (truncation). Deep ITM calls misprice.
choices: The asymptotic BC: as S→∞, C → S - Ke^{-r(T-t)} (deep ITM call ≈ forward) — NOT zero! V(S_max)=0 is a put's BC (or a call's at S=0). Truncation needs the CORRECT asymptotic: impose the far-field behavior (Dirichlet with S-Ke^{-rτ}, or Neumann ∂V/∂S=1). Wrong BCs poison the whole grid (elliptic/parabolic regularity spreads the error inward). The fix: S_max large AND correct asymptotic BC. BCs are the contract — wrong contract, wrong price.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. The far-field analysis: C(S,t) ~ S - Ke^{-r(T-t)} as S→∞ (intrinsic + time value of strike). Imposing 0 creates a boundary layer of error that diffuses inward — the whole grid suffers. This is the general BC lesson: truncation boundaries need asymptotic analysis, not convenient values. For puts: V(0,t) = Ke^{-rτ} (not 0!). Each product's BCs come from its economics.
scenarios.hint: What is the call's far-field behavior?
evidence: Far-field: C ~ S - Ke^{-rτ}. Wrong BC poisons the grid.

domains.name: Numerical Methods
domains.description: Floating-point arithmetic, root finding, quadrature, and the numerical analysis behind every computation.

scenarios.title: The Vanishing Variance
scenarios.situation: Computing Var via E[X²]-E[X]² on data ~1e8 gives negative variance.
scenarios.prompt: What happened, and what are the fixes?
choices: Catastrophic cancellation: E[X²] ≈ 1e16 and E[X]² ≈ 1e16 — their difference (the variance, ~1) loses all 16 digits to rounding (eps·1e16 ≈ 2). Fixes: two-pass (subtract mean first: Σ(x-x̄)²), Welford's online algorithm (numerically stable single pass), or shift the data. The formula is algebraically right and numerically catastrophic — the distinction that defines numerical analysis.
Variance can't be negative; take abs.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The mechanism: both terms round to ~eps·1e16 ≈ 2 absolute error, but the true difference is ~1 — the error SWAMPS the signal. Welford's recurrence (M_k = M_{k-1} + (x_k - M_{k-1})/k) avoids the large-number subtraction entirely. 'Take abs' hides the disease; float128 delays it (still breaks at 1e16 scale... actually float128 helps but the formulation is still fragile). Reformulate, don't just precision-patch.
scenarios.hint: Why do both terms have absolute error ~2?

scenarios.title: The Oscillating Interpolant
scenarios.situation: Interpolating 11 option quotes with a degree-10 polynomial gives wild swings between quotes.
scenarios.prompt: What is this, and what should you use?
choices: Runge's phenomenon: high-degree equispaced interpolation oscillates (Lebesgue constant grows exponentially). For vol surfaces: cubic splines (local, C², no oscillation) or parametric SVI (arbitrage-aware) — NEVER high-degree polynomials on quotes. The interpolant hits every point and means nothing between them. Shape constraints (monotonicity, convexity → no-arbitrage) further restrict the choice.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. The Lebesgue constant for equispaced nodes grows as 2^n/n — the interpolation operator itself amplifies noise exponentially. Splines are piecewise (local support kills the global oscillation); SVI bakes in the smile's shape and arb constraints. The quant rule: interpolate for LOOKUP (splines), fit parametrically for TRADING (SVI) — and always check the arb constraints on the result.
scenarios.hint: What grows exponentially for equispaced nodes?
evidence: Splines/SVI for surfaces. Lebesgue constant is the warning.

scenarios.title: The Kinked Integral
scenarios.situation: Quadrature on a call payoff's integral converges slowly. The integrand has a kink at K.
choices: Split at K: quadrature rules assume smoothness — the kink (non-differentiable at strike) drops the order. Integrate [0,K] and [K,∞] separately (the first is often trivially zero for calls!). Alternatively: adaptive quadrature (refines at the kink automatically) or transform (integrate in log-strike). The general rule: piecewise-smooth ⟹ piecewise integration. Know the integrand's anatomy — kinks, singularities, oscillations — and split/transform accordingly.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. The order reduction: Simpson's O(h⁴) assumes C⁴ smoothness — at the kink it's O(h) or worse. Splitting restores full order on each piece (each piece IS smooth). For digitals (discontinuous!), splitting is mandatory — no quadrature handles jumps well unsplit. The anatomy-first approach: list every non-smoothness, split there, then quadrature each smooth piece at full order.
scenarios.hint: What order does Simpson achieve across the kink?
evidence: Anatomy first: kinks, jumps, singularities. Piecewise smooth → piecewise quad.

scenarios.title: The Wrong Root
scenarios.situation: Newton's method for implied vol converges — to a negative vol. The price function is fine.
choices: Bad start / straying: Newton isn't bracketed — from a poor initial guess it can converge to a spurious root (or diverge). Negative vol 'solves' the equation mathematically (BS with σ<0 isn't standard but the equation may have solutions). The fix: bracketed methods (Brent) for production, or Newton with a good start (e.g., Brenner-Subrahmanyam approximation) and bounds. Unbracketed root-finding needs supervision; bracketed needs only a bracket.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. The basin issue: Newton's convergence is LOCAL — outside the basin, anything happens (cycles, wrong roots, divergence). Brent's bracketing is the safety: the root is trapped, convergence guaranteed (superlinear with IQI). The quant practice: Brenner-Subrahmanyam (σ ≈ √(2π/T)·C/S) for the start, Brent for the solve — fast AND safe. Never let an unbracketed solver near production market data.
scenarios.hint: What does bracketing guarantee that Newton doesn't?
evidence: Brent: trapped root, guaranteed. Newton: fast but local.

scenarios.title: The Non-SPD CG
scenarios.situation: CG on a non-SPD matrix gives garbage (or breaks down).
scenarios.prompt: Why does CG need SPD, and what do you use instead?
choices: CG minimizes the A-norm of the error — which needs A SPD (the 'norm' isn't one otherwise); the algorithm's orthogonality relations collapse without symmetry. Breakdown (division by zero/negative curvature) is the symptom. Instead: GMRES/MINRES (symmetric indefinite → MINRES; general → GMRES), or fix the matrix (it should've been SPD — the formulation bug). The method-matrix match: SPD→CG, symmetric→MINRES, general→GMRES. Match or break.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The A-inner-product <x,y>_A = x'Ay is only an inner product for SPD A — CG's entire derivation (A-orthogonal search directions, optimality over Krylov subspaces) rests on it. Non-SPD: use MINRES (symmetric, minimizes residual norm) or GMRES (general, restarts for memory). But first ask WHY it's not SPD — often the matrix SHOULD be SPD (covariance, Hessian at min) and the indefiniteness is the real bug.
scenarios.hint: What inner product does CG optimize in?
evidence: SPD→CG, symmetric→MINRES, general→GMRES. Or fix the matrix.

scenarios.title: The Stable Algorithm
scenarios.situation: Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting has error ~1e-14 on a well-conditioned system. Why is it 'stable' despite rounding at every step?
choices: Backward stability: the computed x̂ solves EXACTLY a nearby problem (A+δA)x̂ = b with ||δA||/||A|| ~ eps — the algorithm's errors are equivalent to tiny data perturbations. Then forward error ≤ cond(A) × backward error: for well-conditioned A, the answer is accurate. GEPP is backward stable (Wilkinson); the forward error is the PROBLEM's (conditioning), not the algorithm's. This decomposition (stability × conditioning) is numerical analysis' master framework.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. Wilkinson's backward error analysis: the genius is shifting perspective from 'how wrong is x̂?' (hard) to 'what problem did we solve exactly?' (answerable: a nearby one). Then conditioning takes over: nearby problem + well-conditioned ⟹ nearby solution. The master equation: forward ≤ cond × backward. Diagnose failures by asking which factor broke — the algorithm's (stability) or the problem's (conditioning).
scenarios.hint: What is the master equation of error analysis?
evidence: Stability: algorithm's. Conditioning: problem's. Diagnose separately.

scenarios.title: The Gradient Choice
scenarios.situation: You need gradients of a complex pricing function for calibration. Options: hand-coded, finite differences, AD.
choices: AD (exact to machine precision, no step-size dilemma, scales via reverse mode for many-inputs-one-output). Hand-coded: bug-prone for complex functions (but fine for simple, verified ones). Finite differences: always the WORST choice for gradients (truncation + cancellation, O(n) function evals, inaccurate) — use only when the function is a black box. The hierarchy: AD > hand-verified > FD. The capstone's dual numbers were forward-mode AD; reverse mode (backprop) handles the many-parameter case.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. The FD error dilemma (truncation h² vs cancellation eps/h) means no step size is right — and for n parameters, FD needs n+1 evals with INACCURATE gradients. Reverse-mode AD: ONE forward+backward pass, exact gradients, cost ~2-3x the function. This is why ML uses backprop (reverse AD), not finite differences. For calibration (many params, one objective), reverse mode is the only sane choice.
scenarios.hint: Why is FD always the worst choice for gradients?
evidence: Reverse mode for many params. FD: inaccurate + expensive.

domains.name: Measure-Theoretic Probability
domains.description: Sigma-algebras, Lebesgue integration, conditional expectation, and the rigorous foundation of modern quant.

scenarios.title: The Null Set
scenarios.situation: Two processes are equal except on a null set. A student asks: 'are they the same process?'
scenarios.prompt: What is the working answer, and when does it break?
choices: For integration/expectation/distribution: YES — null sets are invisible (same finite-dimensional distributions, same E[·]). It breaks for PATHWISE statements (continuity of paths! suprema!): 'a.s. continuous' needs a continuous VERSION — Kolmogorov's continuity theorem provides it. The working rule: null sets don't matter for laws and integrals; they matter for path properties. Versions, modifications, indistinguishability — the hierarchy of 'sameness.'
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. The versions hierarchy: modification (X_t = Y_t a.s. for each t) vs indistinguishable (P(X_t = Y_t ∀t) = 1) — for path properties you need indistinguishability from a good version. Brownian motion's construction IS this: Kolmogorov-Chentsov gives a continuous modification. The student must learn: 'a.s.' is the default equality, but pathwise claims need versions.
scenarios.hint: When do null sets matter?
evidence: Invisible to integrals; visible to paths. Versions fix it.

scenarios.title: The Finer Filtration
scenarios.situation: G ⊂ H (G coarser). Compare E[X|G] and E[X|H] as estimators of X.
scenarios.prompt: Which is better, and what does the tower say?
choices: E[X|H] is better (smaller MSE): L²(G) ⊂ L²(H), so projection onto the larger space is closer — more information never hurts (for MSE). The tower: E[E[X|H]|G] = E[X|G] — coarsening the finer estimate recovers the coarser. The variance decomposition: Var(X) = E[Var(X|H)] + Var(E[X|H]) — H explains some variance; the rest is residual. Information has a price in variance explained.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. The projection geometry: bigger subspace ⟹ closer projection ⟹ smaller residual. The tower's direction (fine conditioned on coarse = coarse) is the consistency: the estimates cohere across information levels. The variance decomposition quantifies information's value — E[Var(X|H)] is the irreducible uncertainty after H. This is the mathematics of 'more data helps.'
scenarios.hint: What does the tower say about coherence?
evidence: Projection onto larger space. Tower: coherence across levels.

scenarios.title: The Density That Isn't
scenarios.situation: Q(A) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B) for fixed B. What is dQ/dP?
scenarios.prompt: Compute it and check the conditions.
choices: dQ/dP = 1_B/P(B) — verify: ∫_A (1_B/P(B)) dP = P(A∩B)/P(B) = Q(A). ✓. Conditions: Q ≪ P (Q(A)=0 whenever P(A)=0 — yes, since Q(A) ≤ P(A)/P(B)), and σ-finiteness (probability spaces are finite — fine). This is CONDITIONING as change of measure! P(·|B) is the measure Q with density 1_B/P(B). The RN derivative makes 'conditional probability' a special case of 'change of measure' — the unification.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. The normalization 1/P(B) is essential — without it, the integral gives P(A∩B), not the conditional probability. The unification insight: Bayes' rule, conditioning, and Girsanov are ALL Radon-Nikodym derivatives — different densities, same theorem. 'P(A|B)' was always a change of measure; measure theory just names it.
scenarios.hint: What does this unify?

scenarios.title: The Converging Estimates
scenarios.situation: M_n = E[X|F_n] with F_n ↑, E|X| < ∞. What happens as n→∞?
scenarios.prompt: What theorem, and what is the limit?
choices: Doob's martingale convergence: M_n → E[X|F_∞] a.s. AND in L¹ — the estimates converge to the full-information conditional expectation. If F_∞ = F (everything revealed), the limit is X itself. The UI here is automatic? No — need UI for L¹; a.s. needs L¹-boundedness (E|M_n| ≤ E|X| < ∞ ✓). This is why Bayesian updating 'works': the posterior mean is a Doob martingale converging to the truth (given the model).
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The L¹ bound: |M_n| = |E[X|F_n]| ≤ E[|X||F_n], so E|M_n| ≤ E|X| < ∞ — L¹-bounded, hence a.s. convergence (Doob). The limit E[X|F_∞] is 'X given all eventual information.' Lévy's upward theorem is the same result. The philosophical payoff: learning (conditioning on growing information) provably converges — the mathematics of induction.
scenarios.hint: Why does it converge — what's bounded?

scenarios.title: Why Girsanov Works
scenarios.situation: Z_t = exp(-½∫₀ᵗθ²ds + ∫₀ᵗθdW_s). Why is Z a martingale, and why does that make W^Q Brownian?
choices: (1) Z is a martingale: it's the stochastic exponential (Doléans-Dade) — E[Z_t]=1 under Novikov (E[exp(½∫θ²)]<∞), and Z_t = E[Z_T|F_t] by the martingale property of stochastic integrals. (2) Lévy's characterization: W^Q is a continuous martingale under Q with [W^Q]=t — and continuous martingales with quadratic variation t ARE Brownian motion. The RN derivative's martingale property transfers the BM property across measures. Novikov is the fine print.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. Lévy's characterization is the key: BM ⟺ continuous local martingale + quadratic variation t. Under Q, W^Q = W - ∫θ has [W^Q] = [W] = t (finite-variation part doesn't affect QV), and Girsanov's theorem (via the martingale Z) makes it a Q-martingale — hence Q-Brownian.
